questions.question: What is reflection in Java, what are the real use cases, and what are the risks?
questions.title: Java Reflection — What It Is, Real Use Cases, and the Risks You Accept
questions.direct_answer: **Reflection** is the JVM's API (`java.lang.reflect`) for inspecting and modifying classes, fields, methods, and constructors at **runtime** — without knowing them at compile time. Given a `Class<?>`, you can list methods, invoke them, read/write fields, instantiate objects, and even access `private` members after `setAccessible(true)`. **Real use cases**: dependency injection (Spring, Guice), ORM (Hibernate, JPA reading `@Entity`), serialization (Jackson, Gson mapping JSON to fields), test frameworks (JUnit discovering `@Test` methods), mocking (Mockito). **Risks**: 10–50x slower than direct calls, bypasses compile-time type checking, breaks encapsulation, triggers `InaccessibleObjectException` under the Java 9+ module system unless explicitly opened, and defeats tree-shaking/dead-code elimination.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows what reflection enables, which frameworks rely on it, and the performance/safety costs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking reflection is slow in absolute terms (it's slow relative to direct calls but fine in most cases). Not knowing about Java 9+ modules blocking reflective access to JDK internals
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss MethodHandles (Java 7+) as a faster, type-safer alternative. Mention `--add-opens` module flag as the workaround for Java 9+ access. Know the new `Lookup` API for private access without setAccessible

sections.title: Reflection Is How Frameworks Do Magic — And Where the Magic Comes From
sections.content:
When Spring sees `@Autowired` on a field and quietly injects a dependency, when Jackson converts JSON into a POJO, when JUnit discovers every method annotated with `@Test` and runs it — they all use **reflection**. Reflection is the JVM's API (`java.lang.reflect`) for inspecting and modifying the structure and behavior of code at runtime.

The entry point is `Class<?>`. Once you have one — via `Class.forName("com.x.User")`, `obj.getClass()`, or `User.class` — you can:
- List its methods, fields, constructors, annotations, superclasses, interfaces.
- Instantiate it: `clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()`.
- Invoke any method: `method.invoke(instance, args)`.
- Read/write any field, including private ones after `setAccessible(true)`.

This power is what makes Spring dependency injection, Hibernate ORM mapping, Jackson serialization, and Mockito spy creation possible. Without reflection, every framework would need code generation or manual configuration; with it, frameworks can work generically against any user-defined type.

The cost: reflective calls are 10–50x slower than direct calls (the JIT can't inline through them as easily), the compiler can't check argument types, and you can silently break encapsulation. Java 9+ modules tightened the rules to prevent reflection from reading JDK internals without explicit permission.

sections.title: Basic Reflection — Reading Metadata
The Real Use Cases — Where Reflection Earns Its Keep
sections.content:
**1. Dependency injection (Spring, Guice, Dagger)**: Spring scans classes for `@Component`/`@Service`, creates instances, then uses reflection to find `@Autowired` fields and inject matching beans. Your code never calls `new UserService()` — the framework does it via reflection.

**2. ORM (Hibernate, JPA)**: At startup, Hibernate reflects over each `@Entity` class, reads `@Column` annotations, and builds the object-to-row mapping. At query time it reads each ResultSet row and sets entity fields by reflection.

**3. Serialization (Jackson, Gson)**: To serialize a POJO to JSON, Jackson reads every getter (or field) via reflection, checks for `@JsonIgnore`/`@JsonProperty`, and builds the JSON. Deserialization goes the other way.

**4. Testing frameworks (JUnit, TestNG)**: JUnit scans your class for methods annotated `@Test`, `@BeforeEach`, etc., and invokes them in the right order. Without reflection it would need a base class or explicit registration per test.

**5. Mocking (Mockito)**: `Mockito.mock(Foo.class)` generates a proxy class at runtime that intercepts every method call. Implementation uses bytecode generation (ByteBuddy) + reflection.

**6. Configuration binding (Spring `@ConfigurationProperties`)**: Reads property files, matches keys to field names by reflection, applies type conversion.

**7. Plugin systems**: Load a JAR at runtime, discover classes implementing a known interface, instantiate and register them.

In all of these, reflection is the escape hatch that lets the framework work without knowing the user's types in advance.

sections.title: The Risks — Performance, Type Safety, Encapsulation, Modules
sections.content:
**Performance**: reflective calls are 10–50x slower than direct calls. The JVM can't inline through `Method.invoke()` as aggressively, and argument boxing (every primitive becomes an `Object[]`) adds allocation cost. Fine for framework init (once per startup); bad for hot loops.

**Type safety**: the compiler can't verify your reflective calls. Wrong method name, wrong argument types — you only find out at runtime via `NoSuchMethodException` or `InvocationTargetException`. Refactoring tools may miss reflective references entirely.

**Encapsulation**: `setAccessible(true)` lets you read/write private fields and call private methods. Useful for testing but a landmine in production — a library that reaches into private state breaks when the internal representation changes between versions.

**Java 9+ module system (JPMS)**: reflective access to JDK internals or unopened modules now throws `InaccessibleObjectException`. Libraries that reflected on `sun.misc.Unsafe` or `java.util.ArrayList`'s internals suddenly broke. The fix is `--add-opens java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED` at launch, or updating the library to use `MethodHandles.Lookup` with proper lookup class.

**Security**: untrusted code with reflection access can bypass checks. Historically a source of sandbox escapes. Java's `SecurityManager` (being deprecated) tried to contain this; modern Java relies on the module system instead.

sections.title: Reflection vs `MethodHandles` vs Code Generation
sections.content:
**Reflection (`java.lang.reflect`)**
- Pros: ubiquitous, simple API, available since Java 1.1.
- Cons: slow, not type-safe, breaks modules, `setAccessible` headaches.
- Use when: framework init time, low-frequency calls, simplicity matters more than speed.

**`MethodHandles` (Java 7+, `java.lang.invoke`)**
- Pros: 2–5x faster than reflection after warm-up, JIT-friendly, type-safe at invocation.
- Cons: more complex API, harder to cache, not intuitive.
- Use when: hot-path dynamic dispatch in frameworks; Spring's auto-configuration uses it.

**Code generation at build time (Java APT, annotation processors)**
- Pros: zero runtime cost, compile-time error checking.
- Cons: longer build times, generated code visible in builds.
- Use when: performance-critical frameworks (Dagger 2, Micronaut, Quarkus) that want zero runtime reflection.

**Bytecode generation (ByteBuddy, ASM)**
- Pros: full control, near-native performance.
- Cons: complex, library-specific.
- Use when: creating proxies, interceptors, runtime class synthesis (Mockito, Hibernate proxies).

**Modern frameworks' direction**: Quarkus, Micronaut, and GraalVM native-image reduce reliance on reflection to enable ahead-of-time compilation — reflection is difficult to analyze statically. If you're building for native compilation, design your app to minimize reflection use.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Reflection** = runtime API to inspect/modify classes, fields, methods, constructors via `java.lang.reflect`.
- **Entry point is `Class<?>`** — obtained from `obj.getClass()`, `Type.class`, or `Class.forName(name)`.
- **`setAccessible(true)`** bypasses access control for private members.
- **Real use cases**: Spring DI, Hibernate ORM, Jackson JSON, JUnit test discovery, Mockito, plugin systems, `@ConfigurationProperties`.
- **Risks**: 10–50x slower, no compile-time type checking, module-system access errors (Java 9+), encapsulation break.
- **`MethodHandles` (Java 7+)** are faster and type-safer; **annotation processors** generate code at build time for zero runtime cost.
- **GraalVM native-image** and frameworks like Quarkus minimize reflection for faster startup and smaller binaries.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Reflection is how frameworks work without knowing your code. Given a `Class<?>`, you can list methods, invoke them, read/write fields, and instantiate objects at runtime without knowing them at compile time.

**What reflection lets you do**
- List fields, methods, constructors, and annotations of any class
- Instantiate objects: `clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()`
- Invoke methods by name and argument types
- Access private members after `setAccessible(true)`

**Real use cases — where reflection earns its keep**
- **Spring DI** — scans classes for `@Component`, injects `@Autowired` fields via reflection
- **Hibernate / JPA** — reads `@Entity`, `@Column` at startup; populates entity fields from ResultSets
- **Jackson / Gson** — serializes/deserializes POJOs by reading getters and fields reflectively
- **JUnit / TestNG** — discovers `@Test` methods, invokes them in order
- **Mockito** — creates proxy classes at runtime with reflection + bytecode generation
- **Configuration binding** — matches property keys to fields via reflection

**Risks you accept**
- Performance: 10–50x slower than direct calls; fine for startup, bad for hot loops
- No compile-time type safety: wrong method name or argument type surfaces only at runtime
- Module system (Java 9+): reflective access to JDK internals throws `InaccessibleObjectException` without explicit `--add-opens`
- Encapsulation break: `setAccessible(true)` reaches into private state, couples you to implementation details

**Modern alternatives**
- **`MethodHandles` (Java 7+)**: 2–5x faster than reflection, type-safer at invocation
- **Annotation processors / APT**: generate code at build time; zero runtime reflection cost (Dagger 2, Micronaut, Quarkus approach)
- **Bytecode generation (ByteBuddy, ASM)**: create classes at runtime with near-native performance

**Recommendation:** Use reflection when frameworks need it — Spring, Jackson, JUnit, Mockito — but don't reach for it in application code unless you're writing a framework. For performance-critical dynamic dispatch, prefer `MethodHandles`. If you're targeting GraalVM native-image or fast startup, design to minimize reflection use — modern frameworks like Quarkus and Micronaut do this by shifting work to compile time via annotation processors.

questions.title: Java Reflection — Inspecting and Manipulating Classes at Runtime
questions.question: What is Java Reflection, what are its use cases, and what are its limitations?
questions.direct_answer: **Reflection** is Java's API for inspecting and manipulating classes, methods, fields, and constructors **at runtime**, even when their types aren't known at compile time. Access the entry point via `Class<?>` — `obj.getClass()`, `Foo.class`, or `Class.forName("com.foo.Bar")`. Use cases: **framework internals** (Spring DI wires beans by inspecting `@Autowired` fields; Jackson reads `@JsonProperty`; Hibernate maps `@Entity` fields to columns), **testing** (Mockito creates mock subclasses; JUnit finds `@Test` methods), **serialization**, **annotation processing at runtime**, and **plugin systems** (load classes by name). Costs: **10-100× slower** than direct calls (though `MethodHandle` closes the gap), **breaks encapsulation** (`setAccessible(true)` bypasses `private` — restricted in Java 17+ by the module system), **no compile-time type safety**, and **harder for the JIT to inline**. Rule: use reflection only when necessary (frameworks, generic tooling), never in hot paths in application code.

sections.title: Reflection — The Framework's Secret Weapon
sections.content:
**Reflection** is Java's API for doing things at **runtime** that are normally determined at **compile time**: looking up classes by name, reading and writing private fields, invoking methods you don't statically know exist, finding all fields annotated with a given annotation, discovering generic type parameters. It's how Spring knows to inject a `UserRepository` into your `UserService` just because you marked it `@Autowired`. It's how Jackson serializes any POJO without you implementing an interface. It's how Mockito creates fake subclasses on the fly.

Reflection's entry point is **`java.lang.Class`**. Once you have a `Class<?>` object, you can navigate to everything else — fields, methods, constructors, annotations, the superclass chain, implemented interfaces. The three ways to get a `Class`:

```java
Class<?> c1 = myObj.getClass();                  // from an instance
Class<MyType> c2 = MyType.class;                  // literal (preferred — type-safe)
Class<?> c3 = Class.forName("com.example.Foo");   // from a string (for plugin-style loading)
```

The broader reflection API spans several packages: `java.lang.reflect.*` (`Field`, `Method`, `Constructor`, `Proxy`), `java.lang.annotation.*` (annotation meta-types), and `java.lang.invoke.*` (`MethodHandle` — a faster, more flexible alternative introduced with invokedynamic). Modern Java emphasizes `MethodHandle` for performance-critical paths; classic reflection remains for framework-style inspection.

The tension in reflection: it's **powerful** because it lets you write code that adapts to types it knows nothing about at compile time, and it's **dangerous** for the same reason — the compiler can't help you catch mistakes, performance is worse, and you're bypassing the access-control system designed to enforce encapsulation.

Framework Use Cases — Real Reflection in Action

Key Points
sections.content:
- **Reflection** inspects and manipulates classes/methods/fields at runtime.
- **Entry point**: `Class<?>` — via `obj.getClass()`, `Type.class`, or `Class.forName()`.
- **Framework uses**: Spring DI, Jackson, Hibernate, JPA, Mockito, JUnit.
- **Performance**: 10-100x slower than direct calls; `MethodHandle` is ~2-3x slower and often JIT-inlined.
- **Cache reflection objects** outside hot loops — don't re-resolve per call.
- **`setAccessible(true)`** bypasses `private` — required for framework DI but breaks encapsulation.
- **Java 9+ module system** restricts reflective access; `--add-opens` is the workaround.
- **`MethodHandle`** (`java.lang.invoke`) is the modern, faster alternative for performance-critical paths.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Reflection** is Java's API for doing at runtime what's normally determined at compile time — looking up classes by name, reading and writing private fields, invoking methods, and discovering annotations. The entry point is `java.lang.Class`, and the core types are `Field`, `Method`, `Constructor`, and `Annotation`.

**Why it matters**: every serious Java framework uses reflection. Spring injects `@Autowired` fields by reflecting on bean classes. Jackson serializes POJOs by reading field annotations. Hibernate maps `@Entity` fields to database columns. Mockito creates mock subclasses. JUnit discovers `@Test` methods. Without reflection, every framework would require you to implement a special interface — the 'magic' of modern Java DI depends on reflection.

**Costs**: reflection is **10 to 100 times slower** than direct calls — argument boxing, permission checks, indirect dispatch. For hot paths, cache the `Method` or `Field` object so you don't re-resolve per call. For truly performance-sensitive code, use `MethodHandle` from `java.lang.invoke` — it's much closer to direct-call speed and often JIT-inlined.

**Encapsulation**: reflection can bypass `private` with `setAccessible(true)`. In **Java 9 and the module system**, this is restricted on JDK-internal types. In **Java 17+**, application modules also restrict reflective access unless they declare `opens` in `module-info.java`. The workaround is `--add-opens` on the command line — a common issue when upgrading legacy apps to modern Java.

**When to use reflection in your own code**: rarely. For framework code, generic tooling, or plugin systems — absolutely. For application code, prefer direct calls. If you find yourself reaching for reflection in a service, there's probably a design issue — an interface, generic type, or strategy pattern that would work better.

The modern alternative worth knowing: **`MethodHandle`** and the `java.lang.invoke` package — faster, more flexible, and the mechanism lambdas themselves use under the hood.

questions.question: Why is Java reflection slow? Compare `Method.invoke` to direct calls, `MethodHandle`, and `LambdaMetafactory`.
questions.title: Java Reflection Performance — Why It's Slow and What `MethodHandle` / `LambdaMetafactory` Do Differently
questions.direct_answer: **`Method.invoke` is ~10–50x slower** than a direct call for three reasons: (1) every call goes through a security/accessibility check unless cached; (2) primitive arguments are **boxed into `Object[]`**; (3) the JIT can rarely inline through `invoke`, blocking method-level optimizations. **`MethodHandle`** (Java 7+) is faster — usually 2–5x slower than direct after warm-up — because it exposes call-site details to the JIT via `invokedynamic`. **`LambdaMetafactory`** is the fastest option: it generates a tiny class that calls the target directly, producing near-zero overhead. **Practical guidance**: reflection is fine at framework init time (once per startup). For hot paths, cache `MethodHandle`s or use `LambdaMetafactory` to produce a `Function`/`Supplier` you can call like a direct reference.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the three distinct reasons reflection is slow, the faster alternatives, and can articulate when each is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming reflection is 'slow' without numbers or reasons. Not knowing `MethodHandle` exists. Forgetting that `setAccessible(true)` + caching mitigates much of the cost
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Benchmark numbers from JMH (direct ~1ns, reflective ~50ns, MethodHandle ~5ns, LambdaMetafactory ~1-2ns post-warmup). Mention that Spring 5+ uses `LambdaMetafactory` for `@Autowired` setter injection for speed

sections.title: Reflection Is "Slow" — But Slow Compared to What, and Why?
sections.content:
"Reflection is slow" is the common wisdom, but the interview-ready version explains **why**. Three distinct costs stack up on every `Method.invoke` call:

**1. Accessibility and security checks.** Each call verifies caller permissions and module-system access unless you cache the `Method` object with `setAccessible(true)` already applied.

**2. Argument boxing.** `Method.invoke(Object obj, Object[] args)` forces every primitive argument to be boxed into an `Object` wrapper. Calling `int add(int, int)` reflectively allocates `Integer.valueOf()` for each argument, burning cycles and adding GC pressure.

**3. JIT inlining is blocked.** The JIT is extraordinarily good at inlining direct call sites. Reflective calls go through `Method.invoke` which uses internal dispatch tables and bytecode the JIT can't fully analyze through. The target method doesn't get inlined into its caller, which defeats further optimizations like escape analysis and loop unrolling.

**Rough numbers (from JMH benchmarks)**:
- Direct call: ~1 ns per invocation.
- Reflective call (`Method.invoke` with cached, accessible Method): ~30–80 ns.
- `MethodHandle.invoke` / `invokeExact` after warm-up: ~5–10 ns.
- `LambdaMetafactory`-generated `Function.apply`: ~1–2 ns, effectively native.

The 30–80x gap between direct and reflection is what makes reflection a bad choice for hot loops — and a perfectly fine choice for framework startup code that runs once per class.

sections.title: Why `Method.invoke` Is Slow — Three Distinct Costs
sections.content:
**1. Access check**
```java
Method m = User.class.getDeclaredMethod("getName");
for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) {
    m.invoke(user); // every call checks access
}
```
Call `m.setAccessible(true)` once and the per-call access check is skipped — removes a chunk of the overhead.

**2. Argument boxing**
`Method.invoke` has signature `Object invoke(Object obj, Object... args)`. Primitives must be boxed:
```java
Method add = Calculator.class.getMethod("add", int.class, int.class);
add.invoke(calc, 1, 2); // autoboxing: Integer.valueOf(1), Integer.valueOf(2)
```
Each call allocates two `Integer` objects (small integer cache helps for ≤127). Multiplied across millions of calls, the allocation pressure becomes real.

**3. JIT can't inline through it**
Reflective calls go through `NativeMethodAccessorImpl` or `GeneratedMethodAccessor`. The JIT sees the call as opaque — it can't know which concrete method `invoke` dispatches to at each call site, so it can't inline the target, perform escape analysis, or unroll loops containing reflective calls.

**Cumulative result**: reflection's overhead isn't one big cost — it's three small costs that compound. Caching the `Method` and calling `setAccessible(true)` once gets you close to 2–3x overhead; without caching, it's easily 10–50x.

sections.title: `MethodHandle` — Faster, Type-Safer Alternative
`LambdaMetafactory` — The Fastest Option
Mitigations You Can Apply Without Switching Away From Reflection
sections.content:
**Cache the `Method`/`Field`/`Constructor` objects.** Don't call `clazz.getMethod(...)` on every invocation — look it up once at startup and store it. Lookup is 10–100x slower than invocation.

**Call `setAccessible(true)` once and cache.** The accessibility check is per-invocation unless suppressed.

**Batch operations by class.** If you're reading N fields of the same class, get all field handles once, then iterate. Amortizes the lookup cost.

**Use `getDeclaredFields()` + caching over `getField(name)` per call.** Listing once and indexing beats named lookup in loops.

**Avoid reflection in tight loops.** If profiling shows reflection in a hot path, replace with `MethodHandle` or `LambdaMetafactory` at that specific call site.

**Consider annotation processors.** For frameworks, generate accessor code at compile time (like Dagger 2, Micronaut, MapStruct) — zero runtime cost, but longer build times and more generated code.

**GraalVM native-image** compiles ahead-of-time with limited reflection support. If you target native, design to minimize reflection or use reflection configuration hints.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Reflection is 10–50x slower** than direct calls; specifically slow because of access checks, argument boxing, and blocked JIT inlining.
- **`setAccessible(true)` once + caching the `Method`** cuts most of the per-call overhead.
- **`MethodHandle` (Java 7+)** is 2–5x slower than direct — JIT-friendly, type-safer, uses `invokedynamic`.
- **`LambdaMetafactory`** generates adapter classes achieving near-direct-call performance (1–2 ns).
- **Rough JMH numbers**: direct ~1 ns, reflection ~30–80 ns, `MethodHandle` ~5–10 ns, `LambdaMetafactory` ~1–2 ns.
- **Init-time reflection is fine**; hot-path reflection is a profile-first target for optimization.
- **Annotation processors** generate code at build time for zero runtime cost — the modern high-performance approach (Dagger, Quarkus, MapStruct).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Reflection is slow for three stackable reasons — and knowing each one is how you pick the right mitigation.

**The three costs of `Method.invoke`**
- **Access check** on every call unless you cached the Method with `setAccessible(true)` already applied
- **Argument boxing** — primitives become `Object[]`; `int` arguments allocate `Integer` per call
- **JIT can't inline** through `Method.invoke` — the target method stays opaque; no loop unrolling, no escape analysis

**Rough JMH numbers**
- Direct call: ~1 ns
- Reflection with cached Method + setAccessible: ~30–80 ns (~30x slower)
- `MethodHandle` after JIT warm-up: ~5–10 ns
- `LambdaMetafactory`-generated `Function.apply`: ~1–2 ns, essentially native

**`MethodHandle` (Java 7+)**
- Uses `invokedynamic` so the JIT can see and optimize the call site
- No per-call access check; primitive handles avoid boxing
- Trade-off: `invokeExact` requires exact type match — more rigid, but that's what enables the optimization

**`LambdaMetafactory`**
- Generates a tiny adapter class at startup that calls the target directly
- Result is a regular `Function` or `Supplier` — you call it like any normal method reference
- Spring 5+ uses this for `@Autowired` setter injection

**Mitigations without changing APIs**
- Cache the `Method`/`Field`/`Constructor` — lookup is 10–100x slower than invocation
- `setAccessible(true)` once, then invoke many times
- Avoid reflection inside tight loops — move it to init time

**Modern alternatives**
- **Annotation processors (Dagger, Micronaut, MapStruct)** generate accessor code at compile time — zero runtime cost
- **GraalVM native-image** compiles ahead-of-time with limited reflection — design to minimize reflection or use configuration hints

**Recommendation:** Reflection at framework startup is fine — the cost amortizes across the application lifetime. For hot paths, profile first: if reflection shows up in top-10 CPU samples, cache `MethodHandle`s or use `LambdaMetafactory` to produce a direct-call-speed `Function`. And for new framework code that needs high throughput, consider annotation processors — they trade build time for zero runtime cost, which is the right call for most performance-sensitive use cases.

sections.title: Annotations — Metadata That Other Code Reads
sections.content:
An **annotation** is metadata attached to a Java element (class, method, field, parameter). It doesn't change the code's direct behavior — it's a marker that **other code** can read and act on. The 'other code' is the framework, annotation processor, or bytecode manipulator that understands what your annotation means.

Java has three built-in categories of annotations:

1. **Language annotations** (`@Override`, `@Deprecated`, `@SuppressWarnings`) — read by the compiler.
2. **Standard framework annotations** (`@FunctionalInterface`, `@SafeVarargs`) — read by the compiler for structural checks.
3. **Custom annotations** — yours or the framework's (`@Autowired`, `@Entity`, `@Test`, `@GetMapping`) — read by whatever tool knows how to process them.

To create your own, you use **`@interface`** (not `interface` — the `@` prefix is the declaration syntax). Parameters of the annotation are declared as methods, optionally with defaults. **Meta-annotations** on the declaration tell Java tools how to treat it.

The key design choice is **retention** — when do you need the annotation to be available? Frameworks like Spring, Jackson, Hibernate need annotations at runtime, so their annotations use `@Retention(RUNTIME)`. Annotation processors like Lombok don't need runtime access — they generate code at compile time and discard the annotation, so they use `@Retention(SOURCE)`. The wrong choice breaks the framework.

sections.title: Declaring a Custom Annotation
Processing Annotations — Three Approaches
Design Decisions — Retention, Inheritance, Parameters
sections.content:
**Retention policy**: pick based on who reads the annotation.

- **`RUNTIME`** — Spring, JPA, JUnit, Jackson, Bean Validation; any framework using reflection
- **`SOURCE`** — Lombok, AutoValue; anything processed at compile time
- **`CLASS`** — rarely the right choice; bytecode tools like ASM can still read `RUNTIME` annotations fine

**`@Inherited` — subtle**: only makes class-level annotations transfer to subclasses. **Does not** apply to methods, fields, or interfaces. So `@Inherited` on a method annotation has no effect — if you want method-level inheritance (common for `@Transactional`-style annotations), you have to walk the inheritance chain yourself via reflection, or rely on framework-specific handling (Spring's `AnnotatedElementUtils` does this).

**Parameters — best practices**:

- **Single value?** Name it `value()` — allows the shorthand `@MyAnn("foo")` without `value = `.
- **Multiple required parameters?** No defaults — caller must provide.
- **Optional parameters?** Provide sensible defaults.
- **Array parameters**: single element can be written without braces — `@Target({METHOD})` vs `@Target(METHOD)`.
- **Enum parameters**: great for constrained choice (`AuditLevel level()`).
- **Class parameters**: common for 'type references' (`Class<?> mapper() default DefaultMapper.class;`).
- **Nested annotations**: supported — `Validation[] validations() default {};`.

**Bean Validation–style composition**: you can put other annotations on yours.

```java
@Target(METHOD)
@Retention(RUNTIME)
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
@Cacheable("reports")
public @interface ReadOnlyReport {}
```

Spring's `AnnotatedElementUtils` understands composed annotations — `@ReadOnlyReport` behaves as if both `@Transactional(readOnly=true)` and `@Cacheable("reports")` were present.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Declare** with `@interface` — parameters are methods with optional defaults.
- **`@Target`** — where it can be used (METHOD, TYPE, FIELD, PARAMETER, etc.).
- **`@Retention`** — `SOURCE` (APT-only), `CLASS` (bytecode), `RUNTIME` (reflection).
- **`@Documented`** — include in Javadoc.
- **`@Inherited`** — transfer to subclasses; **class-level only**.
- **`value()`** parameter enables shorthand `@MyAnn("foo")`.
- **Three processing times**: runtime reflection (Spring, Jackson), APT (Lombok, AutoValue), bytecode (AspectJ, ASM).
- **RUNTIME retention** is required for any framework using reflection to read the annotation.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
You declare a custom annotation with **`@interface`**. Parameters are declared as methods with optional defaults — `String value() default "";`. The single-parameter-named-`value` convention enables the shorthand `@MyAnn("foo")`.

The configuration comes from **meta-annotations**. **`@Target`** specifies where it can be applied — `METHOD`, `TYPE`, `FIELD`, `PARAMETER`. **`@Retention`** controls lifetime — `SOURCE` discards it at compile time, `CLASS` keeps it in bytecode but not at runtime, `RUNTIME` keeps it available to reflection. **`@Documented`** includes it in Javadoc. **`@Inherited`** makes it transfer to subclasses — but only for class-level annotations, not methods or fields.

**The retention choice matters**. Spring, Jackson, JPA, JUnit — all use reflection to read annotations at runtime, so their custom annotations need **`RUNTIME`** retention. Annotation processors like Lombok, AutoValue, and Dagger read annotations at compile time and generate code, so they use **`SOURCE`** retention — the annotation isn't even in the bytecode. Using the wrong retention breaks the framework.

**Processing an annotation** happens in one of three ways.

**First**, runtime reflection — Spring, Hibernate, Jackson. You iterate methods or fields and call `getAnnotation(MyAnn.class)`. Simple, flexible, slightly slower at runtime.

**Second**, compile-time annotation processing — **APT**. You extend `AbstractProcessor`, declare `@SupportedAnnotationTypes`, and generate new Java source files using tools like JavaPoet. Lombok, MapStruct, Dagger, AutoValue all use this approach. Zero runtime cost because the processing is done before the program ever runs.

**Third**, bytecode manipulation — AspectJ, ASM, ByteBuddy. The tool directly modifies `.class` files after compilation. Most powerful, most complex.

For **most custom annotations** you'd write in an application, you want `RUNTIME` retention plus Spring AOP — define an `@Aspect` with `@Around("@annotation(myAnn)")` and your logic runs whenever a method with that annotation is called.

questions.title: Meta-Annotations in Java — `@Retention`, `@Target`, `@Documented`, `@Inherited` Explained
questions.direct_answer: **Meta-annotations** are annotations applied to **other annotations** to control how they're used. The four main ones: **`@Retention`** — when the annotation is preserved (`SOURCE`, `CLASS`, `RUNTIME`); **`@Target`** — which program elements can carry it (`TYPE`, `METHOD`, `FIELD`, `PARAMETER`, `CONSTRUCTOR`, `ANNOTATION_TYPE`, etc.); **`@Documented`** — include in Javadoc output; **`@Inherited`** — subclasses inherit the annotation from the parent class. Java 8+ adds **`@Repeatable`**. **Retention policies**: `SOURCE` = discarded by compiler (Lombok, `@Override`); `CLASS` = in bytecode but not loaded (default; tools); `RUNTIME` = available via reflection (Spring `@Autowired`, JUnit `@Test`).

sections.title: Annotations About Annotations — Controlling How They Behave
sections.content:
When you write `@Autowired`, `@Test`, `@Override`, or `@Deprecated`, each of those is an **annotation** declared with meta-annotations that control its behavior. Meta-annotations live in `java.lang.annotation` and answer questions like: *When should the compiler preserve this annotation? Where in the code can it be applied? Should subclasses inherit it?*

There are four you'll see in nearly every real annotation declaration:

- **`@Retention`** — how long the annotation is kept (SOURCE, CLASS, RUNTIME).
- **`@Target`** — which program elements are allowed to carry it (class, method, field, etc.).
- **`@Documented`** — whether Javadoc includes it.
- **`@Inherited`** — whether subclasses automatically inherit it from parent classes.

Java 8 added **`@Repeatable`** to allow the same annotation to appear multiple times on a single element.

Without meta-annotations, every annotation would have the same default behavior, limiting how frameworks can use them. Understanding these four is what separates "I can annotate code" from "I can design a useful annotation."

sections.title: `@Retention` — The Three Policies That Control Visibility
sections.content:
Every annotation has exactly one retention policy. If you don't specify `@Retention`, the default is `CLASS`.

**`SOURCE`** — compiler discards it after reading the source file. Not in `.class` files, not in the runtime. Examples: `@Override`, `@SuppressWarnings`, Lombok's `@Getter`/`@Setter` (Lombok generates code at compile time, then the annotations disappear). Used when the annotation affects only the compiler or code generation.

**`CLASS`** (default) — retained in the `.class` file but not loaded by the JVM at runtime. Reflection can't read it. Used by bytecode analysis tools (FindBugs, SpotBugs) that work off the `.class` file without loading classes.

**`RUNTIME`** — retained in the `.class` file AND loaded by the JVM. Readable at runtime via reflection (`element.getAnnotation(MyAnnotation.class)`). Required for any framework annotation that works at runtime: Spring `@Autowired`, `@Component`, `@Service`; Jackson `@JsonProperty`; JUnit `@Test`, `@BeforeEach`; Hibernate `@Entity`.

**Quick decision rule**: if your annotation drives runtime behavior (framework reflection), use `RUNTIME`. If it's processed at compile time (code generation, lint), use `SOURCE`. `CLASS` is rare in application code — mostly for bytecode-tool authors.

sections.title: `@Target` — Where the Annotation Can Be Applied
`@Documented` and `@Inherited`
`@Repeatable` (Java 8+) — Same Annotation Multiple Times
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Meta-annotations** apply to **other annotations** to control their behavior.
- **Four main ones**: `@Retention`, `@Target`, `@Documented`, `@Inherited`. Java 8+ adds `@Repeatable`.
- **`@Retention(SOURCE)`**: compile-time only (Lombok, `@Override`).
- **`@Retention(CLASS)`** (default): in bytecode but not loaded to JVM (bytecode tools).
- **`@Retention(RUNTIME)`**: reflection-readable (Spring, Jackson, JUnit frameworks).
- **`@Target`** enforces where the annotation can appear; compile error if misused.
- **`@Inherited` only applies to class-level annotations**; methods and fields don't inherit regardless.
- **`@Documented`** includes the annotation in Javadoc output.
- **`@Repeatable` (Java 8+)** allows the same annotation multiple times via a container annotation.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Meta-annotations are annotations that apply to **other annotations** — they control how the annotation behaves.

**The four main meta-annotations**
- **`@Retention`** — when the annotation is preserved
- **`@Target`** — where it can be applied
- **`@Documented`** — whether it shows up in Javadoc
- **`@Inherited`** — whether subclasses inherit it from parent classes
- Java 8+ adds **`@Repeatable`** for applying the same annotation multiple times

**The three retention policies — pick based on when the annotation matters**
- **`SOURCE`** — discarded by the compiler; not in bytecode. Used for compile-time processing: Lombok `@Getter`, `@Override`, `@SuppressWarnings`
- **`CLASS`** (default) — in the `.class` file but not loaded by the JVM at runtime. Used by bytecode analysis tools like SpotBugs
- **`RUNTIME`** — loaded and readable via reflection. Required for any framework annotation that drives runtime behavior: Spring `@Autowired`, JUnit `@Test`, Jackson `@JsonProperty`, Hibernate `@Entity`

**`@Target` locations**
- `TYPE`, `METHOD`, `FIELD`, `PARAMETER`, `CONSTRUCTOR`, `ANNOTATION_TYPE`, `PACKAGE`, `LOCAL_VARIABLE`
- Java 8 added `TYPE_PARAMETER` and `TYPE_USE` for annotations on generic type parameters and any type use
- The compiler enforces `@Target` — applying in a disallowed location is a compile error

**`@Inherited` is subtle**
- Only applies to class-level annotations — subclasses automatically carry the annotation from the parent
- Methods and fields never inherit annotations regardless of `@Inherited`

**`@Repeatable` pattern**
- Define a container annotation with a `value()` returning an array of the repeatable type
- Mark the base annotation `@Repeatable(Container.class)`
- Read at runtime with `getAnnotationsByType()` instead of `getAnnotation()`

**Recommendation:** For any framework-style annotation that drives runtime behavior, use `@Retention(RUNTIME)` + `@Target(specific locations)` + `@Documented`. Skip `@Inherited` unless you specifically want class-level inheritance behavior — most frameworks do their own discovery logic. Use `@Repeatable` when you legitimately need multiple instances on the same element (schedules, validation groups), not as a workaround for poor API design.

questions.title: Compile-Time Annotation Processing (APT) — How Lombok and AutoValue Work
questions.question: What is Java annotation processing (APT), and how do tools like Lombok use it?
questions.direct_answer: **Annotation Processing Tool (APT)** runs during **`javac`** compilation — it reads annotations on Java source and generates new source files (or modifies the AST) before compilation completes. You implement an **`AbstractProcessor`** declaring `@SupportedAnnotationTypes` and `@SupportedSourceVersion`, and register it via **`META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor`**. The processor runs in **rounds** — each round may generate new source that triggers another round. Tools like **Lombok** (`@Getter`, `@Setter`, `@Builder`) use APT with AST modification (a slightly hacky approach that reaches into `javac`'s internal `Trees` API). **AutoValue** and **MapStruct** use APT the 'clean' way — generating sibling source files like `AutoValue_User.java`. The advantage over runtime reflection: **zero runtime cost** — the generated code is compiled normally, executes at full JIT speed, and doesn't require `setAccessible(true)` or break the module system. The downside: it's compile-time only, so it can't adapt to runtime configuration.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know APT runs during compilation (not runtime), can name tools that use it, and understand it generates code rather than reflecting on types at runtime
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing APT with runtime reflection; thinking Lombok uses reflection (it doesn't — it modifies the AST during compilation)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish clean APT (AutoValue generating sibling files) from Lombok's hack (AST modification via internal javac API); mention the incremental-compile limitations of APT

sections.title: APT — Compile-Time Code Generation
sections.content:
**Annotation processing** is a Java compiler feature that lets you hook into `javac` to read annotations and generate new Java source files **before compilation completes**. It's different from runtime reflection in a fundamental way: by the time your program runs, the generated code is already compiled into ordinary bytecode — no reflection, no proxies, no `setAccessible`, no module-system issues.

The processor runs as part of the compiler, in **rounds**:

1. Compiler starts; parses your source files into abstract syntax trees.
2. Round 1: compiler invokes each registered `Processor`, passing the elements (classes, methods, fields) annotated with types the processor declares it handles.
3. Processors may generate new source files via `Filer.createSourceFile(...)`.
4. If any files were generated, round 2 begins — compiler processes the new sources, running processors again.
5. Rounds continue until no more generation happens. Compilation completes.

**Tools that use APT**:

- **Lombok** — `@Getter`, `@Setter`, `@Data`, `@Builder`, `@SneakyThrows`. Modifies the compiler's AST directly (not strictly clean APT — uses internal `com.sun.tools.javac` APIs).
- **AutoValue** (Google) — `@AutoValue` on an abstract class generates a concrete subclass with equals/hashCode/toString/constructor.
- **Immutables** — similar to AutoValue but richer features.
- **MapStruct** — `@Mapper` on an interface generates a concrete implementation that maps between types.
- **Dagger** (Google) — `@Inject`, `@Component`, `@Module` — generates DI graph wiring code at compile time. Zero runtime reflection (unlike Spring's reflection-based DI).
- **Micronaut** — `@Controller`, `@Inject`, `@Singleton` — processes annotations at compile time to replace Spring-style runtime reflection.
- **Spring Boot configuration processor** — generates `META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json` for IDE autocomplete on `@ConfigurationProperties`.

APT is increasingly important in the JVM ecosystem because it **enables fast startup** and **lower memory** — critical for GraalVM native image and serverless workloads where runtime reflection is either impossible or very expensive.

sections.title: Writing an Annotation Processor
How Lombok Works — A Special Case
sections.content:
Lombok is the most popular annotation processor in the Java ecosystem, but it works differently from AutoValue or MapStruct. Those tools **generate new source files** — you see `AutoValue_User.java` appear in `target/generated-sources`. Lombok instead **modifies the existing class's AST**.

When you write:

```java
@Getter @Setter
public class User {
    private String name;
    private int age;
}
```

Lombok's annotation processor doesn't generate a `UserWithGetters.java`. Instead, it reaches into `javac`'s internal `com.sun.tools.javac.tree.JCTree` API and **inserts `getName()`, `setName()`, `getAge()`, `setAge()` methods directly into the `User` class's AST**. When the compiler continues, it sees those methods and compiles them into `User.class`.

This AST modification approach has trade-offs:

**Pros**:
- Source looks clean — no separate `UserBuilder` class to manage
- Modified class has the methods on itself — no delegation

**Cons**:
- Uses **internal javac APIs** not part of the public compiler spec
- IDE support is **non-trivial** — IntelliJ and Eclipse need Lombok plugins to understand the generated methods during editing
- Breaks occasionally with new Java versions (Java 17's record/sealed support, Java 21's pattern matching — each release has had Lombok compatibility issues)
- **Can't be used with GraalVM native image** without special configuration — the generated methods must exist at image build time

**Lombok alternatives**:

- **Java 14+ records** — replace `@Value` immutable classes entirely. `record Point(int x, int y) {}` is the standard-library answer.
- **IDE live templates** — generate getters/setters with IDE shortcuts; source stays plain.
- **AutoValue** — clean APT approach; slightly more verbose (abstract class pattern) but no internal-API dependency.

Many Java shops have started phasing out Lombok in favor of records + AutoValue for new code, citing GraalVM compatibility and the 'too much magic' concern.

sections.title: APT vs Runtime Reflection — When to Use Each
sections.content:
**When APT wins**:

- **GraalVM native image** — no reflection metadata needed; generated code is part of the image
- **Startup time** — framework wiring happens at compile time, not during `ApplicationContext.refresh()`
- **Type safety** — generated code is checked by the compiler; errors at build time, not runtime
- **Tool support** — IDEs can follow generated code; debuggers step through it
- **No `setAccessible` / module-opens needed** — the code is yours, not an external reflection call

**When runtime reflection wins**:

- **Dynamic behavior** — adapting to configuration only known at runtime (Spring's conditional bean wiring)
- **Third-party class processing** — when you need to annotate classes you don't control
- **Hot swap / class loading** — plugin systems loading JARs at runtime
- **Rapid iteration** — runtime reflection can be changed without recompiling; APT requires a full rebuild

**Incremental compilation concerns**:

APT can slow incremental builds significantly. When a source file changes, the compiler must re-run all registered processors — often re-processing all annotated classes, not just the changed one. Gradle has invested heavily in 'aggregating' vs 'isolating' processor hints to optimize this. Tools like Dagger and Micronaut offer isolating variants.

**Modern JVM framework direction**: both **Micronaut** and **Quarkus** replaced Spring's runtime-reflection DI model with compile-time APT DI. The startup time drops from 5-10 seconds (Spring Boot) to <100ms; memory usage from ~200MB to ~50MB. For serverless and containerized deployments this matters enormously.

**For your own code**, use APT when:

- You'd otherwise write a reflection-heavy framework
- The code pattern is repetitive and mechanical (builders, mappers, getters)
- You need zero runtime cost

For ad-hoc scripts or simple annotation-based cross-cutting concerns (audit logging, retries), Spring AOP with runtime reflection is simpler and sufficient.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **APT runs during `javac`** — reads annotations, generates new source files.
- **`AbstractProcessor`** + `@SupportedAnnotationTypes` + `@SupportedSourceVersion` + META-INF/services registration.
- **Processes in rounds** — generated files trigger new rounds until fixed point.
- **Lombok** modifies the AST directly (uses internal javac API); **AutoValue**/**MapStruct** generate sibling source files.
- **Modern frameworks** — Dagger, Micronaut, Quarkus use APT DI for fast startup, GraalVM compatibility.
- **`@AutoService`** automates the META-INF registration.
- **JavaPoet** — popular library for building source code programmatically.
- **Incremental compile** — APT can slow Gradle/Maven builds; isolating processors help.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**APT — Annotation Processing Tool** — runs during `javac` compilation. You implement an `AbstractProcessor`, declare which annotations you handle via `@SupportedAnnotationTypes`, and register via `META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor`. The compiler runs your processor in **rounds** — each round can generate new source files, which triggers more rounds until no more generation happens.

**The advantage over runtime reflection** is **zero runtime cost**. The generated code compiles into normal bytecode — no reflection, no `setAccessible`, no module-opens, full JIT optimization. For **GraalVM native image** and **serverless**, this is critical — runtime reflection is expensive or impossible, but APT-generated code is just code.

**Tools that use APT**: **Lombok** for `@Getter`/`@Setter`/`@Builder`; **AutoValue** for immutable value classes; **MapStruct** for bean mappers; **Dagger** for compile-time DI; **Micronaut** and **Quarkus** for full application frameworks; **Spring Boot's configuration processor** for IDE autocomplete metadata.

**Lombok is a special case** worth calling out. AutoValue and MapStruct generate clean sibling source files — you see `AutoValue_User.java` appear in your generated sources. **Lombok modifies the existing class's AST** — it reaches into `javac`'s internal `com.sun.tools.javac.tree.JCTree` API and injects `getName`, `setName`, etc. directly into your `User` class. This is why IDE support needs special plugins and why Lombok occasionally breaks on new Java releases — it uses unofficial APIs.

**Modern trend**: frameworks like **Micronaut** and **Quarkus** replaced Spring's runtime-reflection DI with compile-time APT DI. Startup drops from 5-10 seconds to under 100 milliseconds. Memory drops from 200MB to 50MB. For containerized and serverless workloads, that's a huge operational win.

**When to write your own processor** in application code: when the pattern is repetitive and mechanical — builders, mappers, typesafe configuration — and you care about zero runtime cost. For dynamic, config-driven behavior, runtime reflection via Spring AOP is simpler.
